item.title: Why Larry David never wanted this biography made and how a George Costanza scheme won him over
item.description: Author Blake J. Harris talks with Fox News Digital about his authorized biography of Larry David, exploring the comedy legend's career, partnerships and private life.
item.content:encoded:
Larry David spent decades making millions of Americans laugh through his hit television shows, but when it came to his own life story, the comedy legend wasn’t eager to see it in print.

Author Blake J. Harris, who spent six years researching Larry David's life and writing his biography, "Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David," told Fox News Digital that the "Seinfeld" co-creator and "Curb Your Enthusiasm" star had a blunt reaction after reading the manuscript.

"I wanted him to reflect on his career, you know, the 75 years that are in the book. And so I said, ‘Larry, you know, it's been six years. Do you have any big macro thoughts?’" Harris said of the conversation with David.

LARRY DAVID SAW OJ SIMPSON THE DAY OF NICOLE BROWN SIMPSON'S 1994 MURDER: BOOK

"I thought that he would maybe say like, ‘Yeah, it's really so unlikely that I succeeded’ or ‘I really was so unprofessional.’ The things that he had sort of talked about in the book already. But instead, he took the question a little bit differently, and he said, ‘Yeah, if I could do it over, I wouldn't do it.’ Meaning the book, he wouldn't do the book," Harris said.

Despite David's response, Harris said the comedian quickly realized his comment had hurt the biographer's feelings and tried to reassure him.

"The real-life Larry David, who is a pretty sweet guy and has compassion, he noticed that that made me feel bad, and he didn't intend for me to feel bad. So he said, ‘No, no, Blake, not because of anything you did, you did a great job, you did a great job.’ He repeated that, which I appreciated. He said, ‘I just don't want people knowing about me,’" Harris said.

David, 79, co-created "Seinfeld" alongside comedian Jerry Seinfeld in 1989, serving as a writer and executive producer for the show's first seven seasons. The sitcom ultimately ran for nine seasons, with David returning to write the series finale. David later starred in HBO's "Curb Your Enthusiasm," which ran for 12 seasons. The Emmy-winning comedian is widely regarded as one of television comedy's most influential figures.

BARACK OBAMA, LARRY DAVID PARTNER FOR NEW HBO HISTORICALLY BASED SKETCH COMEDY SERIES

But when Harris first set out to write the biography in early 2020, getting David on board was not an easy task. Harris said he initially reached out to David’s longtime collaborator and executive producer, Jeff Schaffer, but David was far from enthusiastic about the idea.

"Larry’s initial response to Jeff Schaffer about me doing the book was, ‘Oh my God, are you kidding me? Why would somebody do this to me?’" Harris recalled. "He was very, very unhappy about this prospect of a book being written about him."

Harris said he believes David's hesitation stemmed from both his desire for privacy and his humility.

"In his mind, he just doesn't see himself as book-worthy," Harris said. "He sees there’s politicians and founders and great world leaders and scientists and all these people who deserve to have books written about them, and he doesn't see himself as one of those people."

WHY EVERYBODY STILL LOVES 'RAYMOND' 30 YEARS LATER: HOW SUBURBAN FAMILY CHAOS BECAME COMEDY GOLD

To break the stalemate, Harris said he took a different approach, one he described as "George Costanza-inspired." After being introduced to David through comedy writer Alan Zweibel, Harris asked Zweibel to tell David he wanted their first phone call to follow one strict rule: He wouldn't ask about either of David’s hit shows. Instead, they would talk exclusively about the New York Yankees.

"Larry and I spoke two days later about the New York Yankees for 45 minutes," Harris said. "And I guess I passed the test, and we started speaking regularly."

Although David began speaking with Harris, he was still hesitant about having a biography written about him.

"I reflected with Larry, who doesn't really reflect all that often. And I said, ‘Is it true that when Jeff Schaffer first told you that I want to write this book about you, that you were not very happy?’ And he said, ‘Oh no, I was so angry. I was so unhappy,’" Harris said.

"And I said, ‘Larry, well, it's, you know, midnight, New York time. It's nine o'clock LA time. Why are you on the phone with me then? No one's holding a gun to your head.’ And he said, the greatest words I've ever heard. He said, ‘I kind of like you.’ And so, Larry David kind of liked me and that sort of gave me the green light to keep moving forward," he added.

JULIA LOUIS-DREYFUS REVEALS ‘TONS’ OF FRICTION BEHIND THE SCENES OF ‘SEINFELD’

Over the course of researching the biography, Harris spoke with hundreds of people, including David's family, friends and longtime collaborators. Among them was "Seinfeld" co-creator Jerry Seinfeld. Harris described the duo as the "Paul McCartney and John Lennon of television."

"In Larry and Jerry's relationship, it was very clear to me, and Jerry conveyed this, that Larry was the pessimist and Jerry was the optimist," Harris said.

Harris explained that while the two were working on "Seinfeld," David would often stare at a whiteboard used to map out episode ideas, worrying that they wouldn't be able to fill it or come up with jokes as funny as those from the previous season.

"This is a thing with Larry even to this day. He's always worried that he's not [going to] be able to come up with as good of ideas as he had in the past, and Jerry would say to Larry, 'Larry, don't worry about 22 episodes,'" Harris said.

Harris said Seinfeld encouraged David to focus on one episode at a time rather than worrying about the entire season.

David expressed gratitude in the book for Seinfeld's ability to "talk him off the ledge" when those doubts surfaced, Harris said. He also learned that the two never had major fights, only minor disagreements over comedic details, including a playful argument over whether former New York Yankees players Moose Skowron or Hank Bauer had the funnier name for a "Seinfeld" script.

"You could just hear Larry and Jerry shouting at each other, 'Moose Skowron!' 'No, Hank Bauer!' in the office. And it was heated in the sense of just joking," Harris said.

"But then at the end of the day, unsurprisingly, they found a way to get both names in the script and both of them got to put their imprint on this. And they never really had any actual fights," he added.

COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT

Beyond David's professional relationships, Harris said one of the biggest revelations from his years of reporting was discovering just how different the comedian is from his selfish television alter ego, particularly when it comes to his family.

On "Curb Your Enthusiasm," David plays a fictionalized version of himself who has no children, a decision Harris said reflected the comedian's belief that parenting was too serious a responsibility to be funny. In real life, however, Harris said David's two daughters are his greatest source of pride, surpassing even his accomplishments on "Seinfeld" and "Curb Your Enthusiasm."

"There's that famous adage to not meet your heroes. I met mine and I left more impressed than when I started," Harris said. "The part of him that we don't see on the TV show is that he's actually kind of a sweetheart. He has a lot of human compassion that’s not expressed on the show. If you were to spend time with him, the very first thing that he would talk about, or the thing that he'd be most proud to talk about, is not ‘Seinfeld’ or ‘Curb’ or even the New York Yankees. It would be his daughters."

Although David was initially reluctant to participate in the biography, Harris said the comedian's objections to the finished manuscript had little to do with unflattering portrayals. Instead, David took issue with passages where he believed he wasn’t funny or came across as too nice.

"The only times that he really had a problem were where he wasn't funny and where he thought he came off as too nice," Harris said.

Ultimately, Harris described David's journey as an unlikely American success story.

"It’s really not just a story about Larry David, it's a story about the 1970s and 1980s comedy scene, it's a story about television and, above all else, it's the story about how this guy who was so unlikely to succeed, but in America, this land of opportunity, somehow, someway, his talent rose to the top, and he was really a late bloomer. So, I think it's really inspiring in that regard."

item.title: Democratic senator-elect calls Trump 'unserious fool' while defending combative political style
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed told Pod Save America that Democrats must treat Trump as an "unserious fool" and stop clinging to outdated political decorum.
item.content:encoded:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, leaned into accusations of acting cocky on the path to victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers, citing a need to push back on President Donald Trump’s manner of communication during an appearance on Pod Save America.

"Long ago, you predicted that you would win this race by seven points, which at the time seemed like a pretty cocky and ill-considered thing to say. Then you won the race by seven points. People are still calling you cocky," podcast host Jon Favreau said during his interview with El-Sayed.

"How do you see yourself?"

"I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed replied.

EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE

El-Sayed’s response sheds light on his view of his own campaign and the tone that he believes Democrats need to adopt to counter Trump’s presence in American politics. It also raises questions of whether El-Sayed’s campaign strategies will yield results in Congress.

In his view, Trump has changed the style of acceptable communication. In turn, he accused Democrats of being hesitant to abandon a kind of decorum to fight fire with fire.

"I just think there’s a responsibility for us to walk out of 'The West Wing' episode that our politics used to feel like and into the reality of where we are," El-Sayed said, referring to a a television drama known for its idealistic portrayal of American politics.

"I say that because if you’ve ever watched a bully in a room, if you don’t stand up to the bully, it’s not like the bully will just go away. The bully just gets stronger," El-Sayed said.

During his campaign, El-Sayed repeatedly pointed a finger at Trump for, in his view, ushering in a new age of political rhetoric. But that view also preceded his Senate bid.

TRUMP DOMINATES EL-SAYED'S ATTACKS AGAINST ROGERS, BUT GOP RIVAL OFFERS UNEXPECTED POLICY SPLIT

He once accused President Donald Trump of inciting terrorism in a 2020 interview, citing a foiled plot to kidnap Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

"These are terrorists; we have to call them that. We have to recognize that that is what the face of terrorism looks like right now. We have to step up against it," El-Sayed said.

"We gotta ask: why are these people getting radicalized? Well, there must be some radical, extremist cleric out there who may be tweeting up a storm about all the things that they think need to be done, like liberating Michigan."

Although President Donald Trump did not call for any kind of violence against Whitmer, El-Sayed said he believed the president was at least partially responsible, pointing to a tweet Trump had made six months before the discovered plot.

"LIBERATE MICHIGAN!" Trump wrote in a post on Twitter, the social media platform now known as X. The post was one of a series calling to "liberate" Virginia and Minnesota from COVID-19 restrictions imposed by Democratic governors.

According to FBI comments to local media, the plot originated before Trump's post.

Even so, El-Sayed called the posts emblematic of a cultural toxicity that had made violence more likely.

"The idea that people would threaten her safety because she was willing to stand up to keep us all healthy is, to me, the example of what the kind of toxicity that we see out of Donald Trump creates," El-Sayed said.

MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

A spokesperson for El-Sayed did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether he believed in a red line for what kind of rhetoric Democrats should refrain from using.

Having won his U.S. Senate election, El-Sayed will be sworn into office on Jan. 3, 2027, the start of the 120th Congress.

item.title: TREY GOWDY: The midterms were a painful lesson that Republicans can't skip learning
item.description: How do you go from winning the Electoral College and the popular vote in 2024 and being trusted with the gift to govern to historic losses in a relatively short period of time?
item.content:encoded:
PROGRAMMING ALERT: Watch Trey Gowdy discuss this topic and more on "Sunday Night in America with Trey Gowdy" on Nov. 8 at 9 pm ET.

Losing is the toughest teacher; so tough, you only want to take the class once. For Republicans, Tuesday night was excruciating. Yes, history said, "Be prepared for losses." Yes, the mood of the voters was anger and uncertainty. But I did not talk to anyone who was prepared for what happened, either in terms of the sheer loss or the margin of the loss.

Senate candidates in red states lost by unheard-of numbers. Long-serving and hard-working Republican House members like Virginia Foxx, Mike Turner and Richard Hudson were caught up in the tidal wave. South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Ohio are red states in most presidential cycles. Not last Tuesday night. It was as thorough a whipping as I can recall in my lifetime. So why? What are the lessons to be learned, and what are the cautions for the Democrats? As it turns out, there are parallels between the two.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

How do you go from winning the Electoral College and the popular vote in a presidential race and being trusted with the gift to govern to historic losses in a relatively short period of time? President Trump did so and easily could claim a "mandate" on certain issues when he was victorious in November 2024. People want a secure border. People want violent offenders deported without delay. People want a rational immigration policy that rewards the right people and is rooted in fundamental humanity. By humanity, I mean showing dignity to those women and men who have been cutting the lawns, cleaning the hotel rooms and working in service industries while also abiding by our criminal laws. By humanity, I mean protecting American citizens from violent criminals – legally here or otherwise.

President Trump’s first DHS secretary wrote last Tuesday night, "We lost because we were ‘too successful.’" It is that type of thinking that turns a one-cycle loss into decades of minority status. When people voted for border security, they were not including glitzy, self-serving ad campaigns focused on boosting personal political ambitions. When people chose Donald Trump in 2024, they gave not one thought to the possibility that Americans would be shot in cars or on the street and labeled domestic terrorists before even an initial investigation was conducted. It is absurd to assert Republicans lost in South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina and Michigan because "we were too successful." Losing can teach you. But only if you bother to show up for class.

Every win is not a mandate. Every mandate is not a license to do whatever you want, regardless of the issue. President Trump was elected in 2024 because he promised to make life more affordable and safer for hard-working Americans who need not worry about the California billionaire tax. They are simply trying to raise families and meet their societal and familial obligations. There was not even a whiff in the 2024 exit polls about voters clamoring for those in government to engage in more self-enrichment, pursue naked personal political ambition, or use public office for anything other than true public service.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

The forensic pathologists were up early Wednesday morning performing their autopsies. Some blamed the war in Iran for being deeply unpopular. Good. War should be unpopular and rarely waged. But being unpopular and being incorrect are two different things. There was no war with Iran. There were nights of strikes, a heroic pilot rescue, and blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. American service members lost their lives as a direct consequence of Iranian action, but that has been the case for decades. Iran has been killing Americans and giving aid and comfort to those who do so for nearly 50 years. That is precisely why the president insisted, "No more" and "No nuclear Iran."

People can take whatever position they like on those issues, and reasonable minds can differ even within the same political party. But let us not forget that Iran has been a global pariah for nearly half a century, and I have yet to meet the person (outside of a few terrorist groups) who thinks it is a good idea for theocratic despots to have nuclear weapons.

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

What is just as plausible is that voters got vertigo from all the fits and starts. War was on and then off. There was peace but then missiles. There was an MOU that took longer to draft than it lasted in effect. Was it possible Americans needed to be convinced that all other means of reining Iran in had been explored and exhausted?

What is just as plausible is that the American people coveted a deeper explanation of why engagement with Iran was necessary now. Perhaps Iran was a drag on the election, but not nearly as much as perceived corruption, higher gas prices, and a sense that no one was listening.

And that leads to the cautionary tale for Democrats. Winning does not equal a mandate. Sometimes it simply means voters hated you slightly less than the other team. With the right candidates, South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, and Georgia can easily be red again. 

Failing to heed the lessons of why you lost, casting blame in all the wrong places, and not engaging in serious self-reflection will most likely prolong that color change.

item.title: Americans who 'screw up' their eating should use a simple fix, says Stanford scientist
item.description: Christopher Gardner of Stanford says legumes like lentils, tofu and edamame are an underutilized source of protein and fiber in healthy diets.
item.content:encoded:
Living a healthy lifestyle is not as complicated as many Americans make it out to be, according to a nutrition scientist, who says people shouldn't try to be perfect but should focus on gradually improving their diet day by day.

"It is simpler than people think," Christopher Gardner, Ph.D., a nutrition scientist at Stanford University and author of the book "Food Sense: What to Eat and Why," told Fox News Digital.

He believes that the 80/20 rule is a solid framework for a healthy diet. The approach encourages people to make nutritious food choices about 80% of the time while allowing flexibility for indulgences the remaining 20%.

NEW PROTEIN RANKING NAMES UNEXPECTED WINNER OVER BEEF, SALMON AND EGGS

Gardner also works with the Stanford Prevention Research Center, where a big part of his role is trying to figure out how to get people to follow guidelines that "everybody knows" but doesn't necessarily follow, such as eating a healthier diet, exercising more and smoking less, he said.

He advises against trying to follow all the latest wellness trends because, sometimes, they're not based on factual information.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

He doesn't recommend cutting out an entire food group or following a strict diet. Rather, he encourages a gradual approach.

An easy way to start improving an unhealthy diet is to incorporate more vegetables, fruits and minimally processed foods.

He emphasized the importance of eating legumes, adding that he feels they're an underutilized component of a healthy diet.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Asian cultures eat a lot of tempe, tofu, edamame and soy, and Latin American cultures eat a whole bunch of bean and grain dishes, and Indian culture eats a lot of lentil dals," he said, noting that legumes are usually inexpensive and versatile.

They're also a great source of protein, Gardner added, as well as fiber, which many people don't consume enough of, he pointed out.

Americans also eat too much junk food, he said, adding that people often know what the healthier option is, but they still choose the "chips and candy and cake and snacks and mocha frappé frappuccino instead of black coffee."

"I don't think the ultra-processed thing is like, oh, we never understood it before, and now we do. I don't really think people know that it's 200 cosmetic additives," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Context matters when determining the "healthier" choice, Gardner noted, using the example of coffee versus tea.

Coffee and tea by themselves are unproblematic, he noted. The issue lies in the sugar, dairy and other ingredients that might be added.

"I can show you volumes of studies that both are good for you," Gardner said, noting that both contain antioxidants, but the additives are what determine which is "healthier."

Ultimately, different things work for different people, Gardner said, and he stays open-minded.

What people eat is much more than just science, he acknowledged, adding that "food is comfort and food is culture and food is other things."

"Whatever you screw up today, you get a do-over tomorrow and the day after," he said, so "give yourself a little grace, a little patience, a little love."

item.title: GOP eyes Senate comeback after Democratic bloodbath, but another political nightmare could await
item.description: Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats Tuesday, but Republicans could flip the chamber in 2028 by sweeping six competitive states and holding the VP.
item.content:encoded:
Republican control of the Senate could return as soon as the 2028 general election, but only if the party can pull off a series of crucial victories in competitive races, a possibility that seems distant following Tuesday night's devastating Democratic sweep.

As of publication, Democrats and independents who caucus with them have secured 54 Senate seats, a total that could grow to as many as 56 pending election calls in Mississippi and Alaska. Assuming Republicans hold the vice presidency in 2028, far from a guarantee, they would need to flip at least four seats during that election cycle to win the Senate back.

While there are ample pick-up opportunities for Republicans in 2028 if the party can return to its typical national performance benchmarks, several vulnerable GOP-held seats could complicate their efforts to retake the upper chamber.

DEMS FLIPS YET ANOTHER SENATE SEAT IN TRUMP COUNTRY AMID SWEEPING GOP UPSETS

Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, for instance, turned 93 in September and faces a decision about whether to seek another term in 2028, when Republicans will be defending his seat in a state where Democrat Josh Turek just defeated Republican Ashley Hinson by roughly four percentage points. His departure before then could also give Iowa's incoming Democratic governor the opportunity to appoint a temporary replacement.

Another possibility that could make the GOP's path back to a majority even more uncertain is the admission of Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., to the union as full states. Such a move would likely require the Democratic-led Senate to abolish or overcome the legislative filibuster, something lawmakers representing more moderate or competitive states may balk at, as well as support in the House and either presidential approval or enough votes to override a veto.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Even if the filibuster is done away with, President Donald Trump could veto admittance bills. Democrats currently lack the numbers to override such a veto.

If Republicans lose the White House in 2028, however, Democrats could have a clearer path to advancing statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., a move that would add four Senate seats and potentially complicate Republican efforts to win back the chamber, though significant political and legal obstacles would remain.

Assuming none of that happens, Democrats will be defending six Senate seats that could offer Republicans potential pick-up opportunities in 2028.

Republicans will have pick-up opportunities in New Hampshire, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio that year. They will, however, be forced to defend vulnerable Senate seats in Wisconsin, Iowa and North Carolina. Indiana, which saw a significant blue shift, also has a Senate seat up for contention in 2028, while Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn mounted a competitive but unsuccessful challenge to Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts on Tuesday, will not hold another regularly scheduled Senate election until 2030.

While 2028 could deliver Republicans a majority if they play their cards right, another defeat on the scale of 2026 could put the Democratic Party dangerously close to the 60-vote threshold necessary to invoke cloture and counter a filibuster.

"It may be unlikely, but I do think it's feasible," Heritage Action government relations director Chip Wyatt told Fox News Digital. "We're just as capable of having a night like the Democrats had on Tuesday in 2028. If anything, that election, the election we had on Tuesday has shown us that two years is a very, very long time in politics. think if you had told anybody in 2024 that this is what happened in 2028, they probably wouldn't believe you."

For Republicans to have a good night in 2028, Wyatt argued that conservatives would have to focus on affordability issues while Democrats overstep their mandate by allowing the fringes of their party to dictate its policy agenda.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz took a similar line in reacting to Tuesday night's election results.

"We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party, not by embracing socialism, but by being real free-market conservatives. The way we built the Texas economic miracle in the first place, and we will build and rebuild America as well," he said. "When the zealots overreach, and they will, we will stand ready to lead in the direction of freedom, of prosperity, of safety and security and common sense. We will return to a new dawn of freedom in America."

2030 features slightly fewer pick-ups for the GOP with a comparable number of states to defend. While Republicans will have pick-up opportunities in Arizona, Nevada, Wisconsin and Michigan, they will also be forced to defend seats in Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

The 2032 election will feature the same regularly scheduled Senate seats contested in 2026, giving Republicans another opportunity to retake deep-red states they blundered this year, such as Kansas and South Carolina. Historically, however, some moderate Democrats have managed to hang on to state-wide offices in typically red states, making a reversion far from a certainty.

Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, for instance, managed to survive multiple GOP challenges in the deep-red state. Kansas and Kentucky, similarly, have Democratic governors that survived Republican challenges in races that received national attention.

While many Republicans, and even some Democrats, have suggested liberal pick-ups in deep red states could be one-cycle wonders, Wyatt cautioned against complacency.

"We should always assume the politicians want to get re-elected and so the senators in the deep red states that have been recently elected as Democrats are going to want to keep their seats and so they're going to be very strategic in how they vote and in what kind of bills they're introducing," Wyatt said. "In some of these deep red states, it's going to be difficult for [Democrats] to hold on to these seats ... Now granted, I've already said two years is a long time, six years is an even longer time. So who knows what kind of political landscape we're looking at in 2032 but Republicans should definitely start off with a strong advantage in many of these states ... But it's never wise to counter chickens before they hatch."

Electoral politics is famously unpredictable. Nobody in 2024, for instance, envisioned South Carolina or Kansas sending Democrats to the Senate in 2026. It is possible that the Republican path to a Senate majority, or lack thereof, will be comparably surprising.

item.title: American war hero details dire living conditions US troops face as Hegseth taps him to 'fix' it
item.description: Dakota Meyer reveals troops going a year without hot water and sleeping in cars as he tours military barracks on Pete Hegseth's Pentagon mission.
item.content:encoded:
Some troops have gone a year without hot water. Others are sleeping in their cars to escape barracks without air conditioning. And some are asking for little more than drywall, spackle and paint so they can make repairs themselves.

Those are among the conditions Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer says he has encountered while touring military installations on a mission from War Secretary Pete Hegseth: Fix a barracks system plagued by decades of neglect.

"I would tell you that there's only a couple that I've seen that are good," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview Thursday.

Meyer, who serves as senior adviser to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force, has visited more than eight installations across the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps since taking on the assignment and plans to visit 30 before the end of the year.

"What I thought was gonna be a professional job very quickly turned into personal," Meyer said.

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

At one installation, Meyer recalled asking a 19-year-old service member what she would change about her living conditions if she could "wave a magic wand."

"If she could just have a hot shower," Meyer recalled. "It's absolutely heartbreaking."

The Pentagon's barracks problems long predate Hegseth and have survived repeated attempts at reform. 

A sweeping 2023 Government Accountability Office investigation documented serious health and safety hazards and found that the department lacked reliable information about the condition of its own barracks, could not determine how much of its facilities spending went toward them and provided insufficient oversight.

Congress and the military services have since committed billions toward improvements, including initiatives ranging from the Marine Corps' "Barracks 2030" to a Navy overhaul of unaccompanied housing. Yet serious problems persist. As of this year, 12 of GAO's 31 recommendations remained outstanding.

Hegseth has sought to centralize the effort under a department-wide task force and accelerate improvements, with Meyer saying the secretary has made clear that identifying problems is no longer enough.

"The secretary has made it clear to me he doesn't expect me to observe this, study it, or to make it better. He expects me to fix it," Meyer said. "And that's exactly what we're going to do."

Meyer, the only Medal of Honor hero to reenlist after receiving the award, said one of his first requests was for Hegseth to give the task force an "authoritative role," rather than simply create another layer of oversight.

The goal, he said, was to give the team the ability "to go out and make decisions, to be able to have impact, to be able to make change, and to be able to direct where that funding goes and how fast it gets to our service members."

EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP

Meyer argued the problem is not simply a lack of money. Funding shortfalls, continuing resolutions and years of deferred maintenance have all contributed, he said, but so have layers of contracting rules and bureaucracy that can slow even relatively basic repairs.

A separate watchdog review found the Pentagon facing a $285 billion maintenance backlog across its broader military facilities' portfolio, underscoring the scale of the department's infrastructure challenges.

"When you look at the contracting aspect, it's easier for people to say no," Meyer said.

Funding is also part of the problem, according to Meyer, who pointed to Congress' failure to enact full-year defense appropriations for fiscal 2027. The Pentagon is currently operating under a continuing resolution through Dec. 11, which generally funds ongoing programs at prior-year rates while lawmakers negotiate a broader spending package.

"When you can't get a budget, when you're waiting on Congress to pass a budget, to be able to get the funding there, I mean, that is a huge issue," Meyer said.

But he also argued that the Pentagon has too often measured progress by how much money has been obligated or put under contract, rather than whether troops actually see improvements in their living conditions.

"Our service members don't, they don't live in our budget lines," Meyer said. "They live in the rooms that those budget lines are there to impact."

For Meyer, that has meant getting out of Washington and hearing directly from the troops living with the consequences.

"You can't fix these problems or understand these problems by standing on the carpet of the Pentagon," he said. "You've got to go out there and talk to these service members."

What he has heard, Meyer said, is striking partly because of how little troops are asking for.

"They're asking for a hot shower. They're asking for a place to wash their clothes. They're asking for a door that locks. They're asking to be able to go to sleep in a place that doesn't have mold. I mean, they're asking for light bulbs."

"They're willing to be part of the solution," he added.

Meyer stopped short of placing the blame solely on installation commanders, saying many want to improve conditions but have been constrained by a system that has normalized poor barracks for years.

"I think this is a multidimensional problem, and it's complex," he said. "I think that you have commanders out there that want to take care of their service members. I've seen that across the board. But ... they still have to have the ability to do that."

Meyer was far less forgiving of previous Pentagon leadership, arguing that years of investments and reform initiatives had failed to translate into adequate living conditions for troops.

"Don't kid yourself," Meyer said. "In the past ... it wasn't a priority to the leadership."

Previous administrations and military leaders did launch barracks improvement efforts and devoted billions of dollars to construction, renovation and maintenance, even as government watchdogs continued to document serious deficiencies.

Meyer said Hegseth has made the issue a personal priority.

"We have the Secretary of War who is putting people first, and he's not just saying that, he's doing it through his actions," Meyer said.

Meyer has put his own name on whether the latest effort succeeds, saying previously that if the barracks aren't fixed, there is "only one person to blame" — himself.

Asked what "fixed" would actually look like, Meyer offered a simpler standard than any Pentagon metric.

"People are living in places that I would be okay for my daughters living in," he said.

item.title: Border Patrol seizes nearly $10M in cocaine during back-to-back California stops
item.description: Border Patrol agents found 550 vacuum-sealed packages of suspected cocaine in two vehicles just three minutes apart at the San Clemente checkpoint.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Border Patrol agents seized nearly $10 million worth of cocaine during two vehicle inspections just three minutes apart at a Southern California checkpoint, authorities said.

Agents discovered more than 1,435 pounds of suspected cocaine valued at $9.8 million during inspections at the San Clemente Border Patrol checkpoint last month, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

On Oct. 25, agents assigned to the San Diego Sector referred the two vehicles for additional inspection after observing "suspicious behavior," including one driver attempting to reverse out of the checkpoint.

A Border Patrol canine alerted agents to both vehicles, leading to the discovery of 550 vacuum-sealed packages concealed inside black garbage bags.

CBP OFFICERS SEIZE OVER $2.8M IN COCAINE AND METH IN BACK-TO-BACK BUSTS AT CALIFORNIA PORT OF ENTRY

Field tests yielded presumptive positive results for cocaine, CBP said.

"With this seizure, we are heading for a record year in narcotics interdictions here at the San Clemente checkpoint," San Clemente Station Patrol Agent in Charge J.D. Scott said in a statement.

"A few years ago, our agents were deployed to the immediate border and processed hundreds of illegal aliens," Scott continued. "With illegal border entries in San Diego at all-time lows, we now have the agents needed to keep our checkpoint open longer and to maintain a strong Border Patrol presence along our I-5 corridor."

CBP OFFICERS SEIZE $67 MILLION IN ILLEGAL DRUGS AT SAN DIEGO BORDER PORTS, DHS SAYS

Both drivers were arrested, and the Drug Enforcement Administration took custody of the suspects and suspected narcotics pending federal prosecution.

The seizures come amid the Trump administration's broader crackdown on drug cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations and human smuggling and drug trafficking networks.

In a separate case in May, authorities in the Southern District of California uncovered more than a ton of cocaine worth an estimated $45 million linked to an alleged cross-border drug tunnel.

item.title: Democrats set sights on Elon Musk probe after midterm wins, but Pritzker draws a surprising line

ELON MUSK BLAMES TRUMP, US MILITARY FOR SPACEX RESTRICTIONS UKRAINE WARNS COULD HAVE DEADLY CONSEQUENCES

"We plan for the worst. We hope for the best. … We always make sure that we are ready to deal with all the challenges or the threats," Al Nuaimi said.

That combination of optimism and caution was evident during Fox News Digital's reporting trip across the Emirates, where daily life appeared remarkably normal despite the uncertainty surrounding the country.

On an evening in downtown Dubai, restaurant terraces were packed, tourists filled the streets and crowds gathered around a fountain show set to music that moved between Arabic songs and Western pop hits.

Businesses were operating, international visitors were arriving and the city continued to project an image of prosperity and openness.

The contrast was just as striking in Abu Dhabi, where Fox News Digital attended the opening of ADIPEC 2026, one of the world's largest energy conferences, against the backdrop of continuing tensions with Iran and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz.

Days before the conference, ExxonMobil and Chevron executives had canceled their planned appearances because of security concerns, Reuters reported on Oct. 29.

Yet inside the exhibition halls, delegates from around the world gathered to discuss investment, announce partnerships and explore technological solutions to the energy crisis.

It was a demonstration of the UAE's determination to keep its economy moving while preparing for a security environment that has changed dramatically.

"Every nation, when it is attacked, [has] the right to defend their people, their sovereignty, their nation," he said.

Despite the confrontation with Iran, Al Nuaimi rejected the suggestion that the UAE's relationship with Washington should be judged primarily through the current conflict or any particular U.S. administration.

"We don't see our relationship with the United States through these conflicts, through security and defense. No, it's a partnership. It's a strategic partnership. It is a sustainable partnership. … Our main partnership is with the United States as a nation, with the American people."

He emphasized that the relationship extends across education, medicine, technology, energy and investment, and is intended to endure political changes in Washington.

"We don't look at the United States through a certain administration. Our engagement and partnership with the United States ... [is] with the nation. It's with the people. ... We have the flexibility and the ability to [adapt] and engage with any administration."

The comments come at a sensitive time for Gulf governments, whose security relationships with Washington have become more consequential as Iran threatens regional infrastructure and international shipping.

At ADIPEC's opening ceremony on Nov. 2, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, emphasized that the country's ability to withstand the crisis was the result of years of preparation. "We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before," Al Jaber told the audience.

The message was consistent with what officials and analysts repeatedly emphasized during Fox News Digital's visit: the UAE intends to remain a reliable international partner despite the possibility of another regional escalation.

In a separate exclusive interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the Emirati research center B'huth, argued that the confrontation with Iran has fundamentally expanded the meaning of national security.

"Our resilience now becomes our deterrence," Baharoon said.

The UAE's security strategy, he explained, involves far more than intercepting missiles and drones. It also means ensuring reliable energy supplies, food security, functioning infrastructure and the ability to maintain international commerce during a crisis.

For Baharoon, the conflict cannot be understood as a single confrontation between Washington and Tehran.

He described three interconnected wars: the initial American-Israeli campaign against Iran, Tehran's subsequent attacks on Gulf states and Iran's disruption of international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

"The second war was Iran's attack on the GCC, because that attack was also unprovoked," Baharoon said, referring to the Gulf Cooperation Council.

He described the disruption of shipping as a separate confrontation with the global economy, arguing that the consequences extend to countries far removed from the Middle East.

Despite his criticism of Tehran, Baharoon rejected the idea that Iran should permanently be treated as an enemy. Its population, economic potential and geographical importance, he argued, could make it an important contributor to regional prosperity if its leadership shifted away from confrontation.

For the UAE, the challenge now is to prepare for the possibility of another confrontation without abandoning the diplomatic and economic relationships it has spent decades building. The crowded streets of Dubai and busy exhibition halls of Abu Dhabi reflect a country determined to move forward, even as the threat of war remains close. Whether the latest negotiations with Iran lead to a breakthrough or another round of fighting, the Emirates is betting that its resilience will allow it to weather the next crisis without losing sight of the future it is trying to build.
